chapter.title: Socrates and the habit of asking why

cards.body: Socrates wrote nothing down, yet in 399 BC Athens put him to death for talking. At our 2,500-year dinner table, he's the guest who never makes a speech. He leans toward whoever sounds most sure, asks **what exactly they mean**, and keeps asking until the food goes cold.
cards.simpler: Socrates never wrote anything down. Still, in 399 BC, the city of Athens put him to death for talking. At our dinner table of thinkers from the last 2,500 years, he's the guest who never gives a speech. He leans toward whoever sounds most sure of themselves and asks **what exactly they mean**. Then he keeps asking until the food goes cold.

cards.prompt: A general at the table says courage means never running from the enemy. Socrates hasn't argued back yet. What does he most likely do next?

options.text: Give a short speech on what courage really is.
Ask about soldiers who retreat on purpose to win, and whether they're brave.
Nod politely and pass the bread.

whyNot.a: That's a lecturer, not Socrates: he rarely offered his own answer first.
whyNot.c: That's good manners, not his method: he stayed on a claim until it held or cracked.

cards.reteach: Socrates worked with questions, not speeches. He found a case the claim didn't fit, then let the speaker try to explain it. The speaker did the work of noticing the gap.

cards.title: Questions as a tool
cards.body:
Socrates spent his days in the *agora*, the open marketplace of Athens, stopping people who claimed to know things: generals about courage, priests about holiness, speakers about justice.

The pattern had three steps. Get a clear claim. Test it with a case. See whether it survives. The Greek name for this is *elenchus*, roughly 'testing by cross-examination'.

You'd think the goal was to win. It wasn't. **The goal was to find out whether someone actually knew what they thought they knew.** Usually they didn't. Neither, he said, did he.
cards.simpler: In the *agora*, the open marketplace of Athens, Socrates stopped people who claimed to know things: generals on courage, priests on holiness, speakers on justice. He'd get a clear claim, test it with an example, and see if it held up. The Greek word for this is *elenchus*, roughly 'testing by questioning'. He wasn't out to win. **He wanted to see if people really knew what they thought they knew.** Usually they didn't. Neither, he said, did he.

cards.title: Euthyphro is suddenly late
cards.body: Outside the courthouse, Socrates meets Euthyphro, who is prosecuting his own father over a worker's death and is sure the gods approve. Socrates asks him what holiness is. Whatever the gods love, says Euthyphro. Socrates asks: is a thing holy because the gods love it, or do the gods love it because it's holy? Euthyphro suddenly remembers he's in a hurry, and **the talk ends with no answer**, which for Socrates still counts as progress.
cards.simpler: Outside the courthouse, Socrates meets Euthyphro. Euthyphro is taking his own father to court over a worker's death, and he's sure the gods approve. Socrates asks him what holiness is. Whatever the gods love, Euthyphro says. Socrates asks: is something holy because the gods love it, or do the gods love it because it's holy? Euthyphro suddenly remembers he's in a hurry. **The talk ends with no answer**, and Socrates still counts that as progress.

cards.prompt: Your flatmate Priya announces: 'Breakfast is the most important meal of the day.' Which reply runs Socrates' method?

options.text: 'Most important for what? And what about people who skip it and feel fine?'
'Fair enough, you know more about food than me.'

whyNot.a: That's a counter-claim, not a question: you've swapped her certainty for yours and tested nothing.
whyNot.c: That's deferring, not questioning: Socrates went to people who claimed to know precisely so he could test them.

cards.reteach: The method asks; it doesn't assert. First get the person to say what they mean, then offer a case that might not fit. A solid claim survives. A shaky one shows its gap, and they see it themselves.

cards.title: Why it cost him his life
cards.body:
Having your answers taken apart in front of a crowd stings. Young Athenians loved watching and copied him. Powerful Athenians did not.

In 399 BC he was charged with disrespecting the city's gods and corrupting the young. A jury of several hundred citizens found him guilty, and he drank hemlock, a poison. At his trial, which Plato later wrote up as the *Apology*, he argued that a life without this kind of questioning isn't worth living.

Now the useful twist: **point the questions at yourself**. You're not trying to prove a belief false. You're finding where its reasons run out.
cards.simpler: Young Athenians loved watching him question people, and copied him. Powerful ones did not. In 399 BC he was charged with disrespecting the gods and corrupting the young. A jury of several hundred found him guilty, and he drank hemlock, a poison. At his trial, written up by Plato as the *Apology*, he said an unquestioned life isn't worth living. Now **point the questions at yourself**, not to prove a belief false, but to find where its reasons run out.

cards.body: Dev tries the method on 'I should answer work email on Sundays.' Why? To stay on top of things. Why does that matter? Dev feels a small wince, decides that's a good enough answer, and stops at question two. Spot it: **the wince is where the questions start being useful**, so keep going until you hear yourself say 'just because' or 'everyone does'.
cards.simpler: Dev tries this on one belief: 'I should answer work email on Sundays.' Why? To stay on top of things. Why does that matter? Dev feels a small wince of discomfort, decides that's a good enough answer, and stops after two questions. Here's the catch: **the wince is where the questions start being useful**. Keep going until you hear yourself say 'just because' or 'everyone does'.

cards.prompt: You ask yourself why five times about 'I need a degree to be taken seriously.' At why number four you answer: 'Because my parents always said so.' What has the method just done?

options.text: Shown where your reasons run out, so you know what to check next.
Failed, because it should end with a clear final answer.

whyNot.a: That's a verdict, not an examination: a belief with a weak reason can still be true; you've only found where its support runs thin.
whyNot.c: That's a finished argument, not the method: Euthyphro's talk ended with no answer, and Socrates still counted it as progress.

cards.reteach: Think of each why as a spade digging one layer down. The layer where your answer turns into 'because someone said so' is the spot to look at next. The belief might still be right; now you know which part needs a better reason.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body:
Socrates tested what people claimed to know by asking questions until their answers held or ran out, and Athens executed him in 399 BC after he'd embarrassed plenty of important people that way. Point the same questions at your own beliefs and you'll find exactly where your reasons stop.

Tomorrow: his student Plato argues the table in front of you isn't the real one.
cards.simpler: Socrates tested what people said they knew by asking questions until their answers either held up or ran out. That habit embarrassed plenty of important people, and in 399 BC Athens executed him. **Turn the same questions on your own beliefs** and you'll find exactly where your reasons stop. Tomorrow: his student Plato argues that the table in front of you isn't the real one.

cards.body: Pick one belief you held this morning, like 'I need coffee to function.' Ask why five times, typing each answer into your notes app. Circle the answer where you first wanted to stop.
cards.simpler: Pick one belief you held this morning, something ordinary like 'I need coffee to function.' Then **ask yourself why, five times in a row**, typing each answer into your notes app. When you're done, circle the answer where you first wanted to stop.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now ask 5 'why' questions in a row about a belief you hold and notice where your answers run out.
